data.name: OESE
data.detailed_description:
OESE is about your little ship, traveling alone through space trying to survive as best as it can to find a new home. Along the journey you come across different encounters with different outcomes depending on your decision. You can either try a passive approach if you're feeling peaceful, you can try to contact or trade with whatever oddity you've crossed paths with or you can go full offensive and fire a missile to try and steal their power!

​OESE is about decisions and consequences.

Features

  • Over 100 different encounters with different outcomes.
  • 7 races and 4 factions that will love you and aid you on your way.
  • 7 races and 4 factions that will hate you and send bounty hunters out to kill you.
  • 20 in game achievements
  • Delicious pixel art and original soundtrack.
  • Customizable ship so you can look nice.
  • The omnipresent impending doom of the indestructible Nox Cubes.
  • A friendly companion to keep you company.

The game is very relaxing and turn-based, allowing you to take your time and enjoy the journey of space (or panic if your power is running low.) If you're in the office or classroom and it's one of those long days that never seem to end then it's rather nice having a little ship to watch over while you get on with your work.

data.short_description: OESE - The space survival game about decisions and consequences.

reviews.review:
OESE is a small-scale space survival game that turns a lonely voyage across the stars into a sequence of choices, resource problems, and unexpected encounters. Developed by Alec Smith and Dane Winn and published by Milo Games, it deliberately avoids the complexity normally associated with space simulations. There are no enormous technology trees or demanding flight controls to master. Instead, the experience revolves around keeping a vulnerable spacecraft operational while deciding how to react to whatever appears during the journey. Its turn-based structure creates a relaxed pace, although the constant possibility of running out of essential resources ensures that there is always some pressure beneath the calm presentation.

The main objective is to travel through space in search of a new home while surviving the encounters scattered along the way. More than 100 different encounters can appear, involving unusual ships, creatures, factions, and other situations. These events typically present several possible responses rather than forcing a single solution. You might behave peacefully, attempt communication, trade resources, or resort to aggression and missiles. Because the outcome of an encounter can influence your supplies and future relationships, even a seemingly simple decision can become surprisingly important.

OESE becomes more interesting through its faction and reputation systems. The universe contains seven races and four factions, and your actions determine how some of these groups respond to you. Maintaining friendly relations can result in useful assistance, while repeatedly behaving aggressively may create enemies. Hostile behavior can even lead to bounty hunters pursuing your vessel. This gives the adventure a sense of continuity because decisions are not always forgotten after an encounter ends. Taking resources through violence might solve an immediate problem, but the consequences can make survival more difficult later.

Resource management provides much of the underlying tension. Power is especially important, and a journey can quickly become uncomfortable when reserves begin disappearing faster than they can be replaced. Since the game is turn-based, however, the pressure comes from strategic uncertainty rather than reaction speed. You are generally free to consider the available choices before committing to an action. This makes OESE approachable while still creating satisfying moments where a risky decision becomes necessary simply because the safer alternative would leave the ship without enough resources to continue.

Another important threat comes from the indestructible Nox Cubes. Their presence helps maintain momentum and prevents the journey from becoming completely comfortable. Survival therefore involves more than simply finding a favorable situation and remaining there indefinitely. The player is encouraged to continue moving, taking chances and dealing with whatever appears next. Failure fits naturally into this structure. Losing a run is less about reaching a conventional game-over screen and more about seeing how long your particular voyage can survive before accumulated mistakes, bad luck, or dwindling resources finally become overwhelming.

The presentation matches the modest scope of the gameplay. Pixel art gives the ships and encounters a charming identity without overwhelming the screen with unnecessary visual detail. Ship customization provides a small opportunity to personalize the vessel, while the presence of a companion gives the otherwise isolated expedition a little additional character. The original soundtrack supports the slower pace effectively, creating an atmosphere that feels more contemplative than dramatic. It is the sort of game that can comfortably be played in short sessions without requiring a major commitment each time.

Replay value comes primarily from discovering different encounters, experimenting with responses, managing faction relationships differently, and attempting to survive longer. There are 20 achievements tied to various parts of the experience, giving completion-minded players additional objectives. At the same time, the game's limitations should be recognized. Its mechanics are intentionally straightforward, so anyone expecting elaborate tactical battles, detailed spacecraft engineering, complex trading systems, or the enormous progression structure of a full-scale space roguelike may find it rather light. Once enough encounters have been seen, repetition can also reduce some of the uncertainty that makes the early voyages appealing.

Steam Deck compatibility is currently not officially rated by Valve, so OESE should be regarded as Unverified rather than officially Verified or Unsupported. Its lightweight requirements and straightforward turn-based design make it conceptually well suited to portable play, but the absence of an official Steam Deck compatibility rating means that controller behavior, interface readability, and other Deck-specific considerations are not formally guaranteed.

Ultimately, OESE is most enjoyable when treated as a compact survival adventure rather than an expansive space simulator. Its mixture of more than 100 encounters, resource management, multiple races, faction relationships, reputation consequences, ship customization, achievements, and persistent threats creates an engaging framework from relatively simple mechanics. The experience can eventually become repetitive and lacks the mechanical depth of larger roguelikes, but its accessible design makes starting another voyage remarkably easy. For players who appreciate turn-based decision-making, unpredictable events, and watching small choices gradually shape a larger survival story, this is a charming journey worth experiencing.

Rating: 7/10
